The authors performed thin-sample directional solidification experiments using a transparent CBr4-1.4 mol% CCl2 alloy with a thermal gradient of 120 ± 20 K/cm.
The nominal constitutional supercooling and Mullins-Sekerka threshold velocities for the 1.4 mol% CBr4-CCl2 alloy are approximately 15 μm/s and 20 μm/s, respectively.
The actual cellular threshold velocity was estimated to be around 15 ± 4 μm/s, which is lower than the theoretical predictions.
At solidification velocities below 6 μm/s, the solid-liquid interface remained planar over the whole width of the sample.
In the velocity range of 6-10 μm/s, a pre-cellulation phenomenon was observed near grain boundary grooves, as predicted by the theory.
Fully developed cellular patterns were observed for solidification velocities greater than 10 μm/s.
Subboundaries exhibit a finite dihedral angle and a much smaller depth of the grain boundary groove compared to high-angle grain boundaries.
The phase-field model uses an anisotropy function a(θ) with smooth but deep minima to approximate a cusp-like behavior in the grain boundary energy.
The Laplacian term is added to the free energy functional as a regularization technique to avoid ill-posedness due to missing orientations in the anisotropy function.
The phase-field simulations demonstrate that the grain boundary mobility plays a crucial role in the observed morphological evolution.
The experimental results are in good qualitative agreement with the theoretical predictions from the previous linear stability analysis.
The findings open an avenue for using directional solidification experiments to obtain information about grain boundary energetics and mobility.
The authors studied the interplay between the diffusion-controlled dynamics of a solidification front and the trajectory of a grain boundary groove at the solid-liquid interface.
The authors used thin-sample directional solidification experiments of a transparent alloy and numerical simulations with the phase-field method in two dimensions.
The authors found that low-angle grain boundaries (subboundaries) with an anisotropic interfacial free energy grow tilted at an angle θ with respect to the temperature gradient axis.
